summary.title: Why writing by hand is still the best way to retain information
summary.one_liner: Handwritten notes support better memory, reading comprehension and recall than typed notes, according to the studies the article cites.
keywords: audrey van der meer keyboard study
takeaways: Handwriting engages memory, visual processing and motor skills more than typing, per the cited studies.
A 2021 University of Tokyo study found people recalled calendar details more slowly from phone entry but recalled faster when writing by hand (25% faster entry by hand).
Early-literacy research (James and Engelhardt, 2012) links printing letters to stronger letter recognition and reading comprehension.
Typed notes can be faster and still useful, but the article argues they do less for later recall.
Practical tip: choose a notebook and pen you enjoy to make a handwriting habit stick.
summary.summary: This Stack Overflow blog post argues that writing notes by hand helps people retain and recall information better than typing. It opens with a work anecdote about a data engineer who missed details from a meeting they had typed notes for, then builds the case through sections on reading comprehension, tactile recall, and the cognitive effects of typing. It draws on cited studies, including a 2012 James and Engelhardt paper on children learning letters, a 2021 University of Tokyo study led by Kuniyoshi Sakai, and comments from Audrey van der Meer. The conclusion is practical: expect handwriting to feel challenging at first and pick a notebook you like.
